title: Paid more than the ceiling on record
question: On which contracts do the payments on record add up to more than the agreed amount, once the obvious data causes are set aside?
finding: 71 contracts, $5.2 million above their ceilings between them; on 59 of the 71 the excess is under 10%, and 1 is over by both 10% and $100,000. The largest is ConvergeOne, Inc. (Technology, Citywide Cisco EA 2019-2026): $65.6 million paid against a ceiling of $65.0 million. Gross vouchers include $2,526,324.82 coded Sales-Use Tax. The other vouchers total $63,030,075.55. Check the signed terms for how the limit treats tax. The raw table suggests far more: read from the prime contractor's row alone, 1,026 contracts look overpaid, but 879 of those are an effect of how the table splits one award across the prime and its subcontractors. Of the 151 that remain when every row is added up, 3 were dropped because the prime's own row is negative, 47 as rents and memoranda and 28 because a neighbouring contract number of the same firm holds the unspent room. A further 37 paid contracts show no ceiling at all, and on 164 the table's own payment column exceeds the ceiling where the payment file does not. 2 more were dropped because the department's own commission records show a larger approved amount than the table does, so the table is out of date: Clark Construction Group - Calif LP (AIR-11918.66-DBCargoBldg626.1): $128.8 million paid, table ceiling $104.2 million, but the Airport Commission's items put the contract at $257.2 million by 2026-05-19; PGH Wong & Partners (AIR-10072.41 -PMSS Courtyard 3): $36.1 million paid, table ceiling $17.2 million, but the Airport Commission's items put the contract at $45.4 million by 2024-01-16.
how: The ceiling of a contract is the sum of the award on every row of the Supplier Contracts table for that contract number: the prime contractor's row holds only the prime's share, and each subcontractor's row the rest. Payments are every voucher in the payment file under that contract number, fiscal 2019 to 2027 to date (payments before July 2018 are not in the file, so older contracts are understated, never overstated). A contract is a candidate when payments exceed the ceiling by more than 0.5% and $1,000. Candidates are then dropped for the causes counted in the finding. The table's own payment column is not used: on some large contracts it repeats amounts across rows.
limits: A ceiling can be raised after the fact: the table shows today's figure, and a payment made under an amendment that has not yet been keyed looks like an excess. Purchases of goods can be invoiced with tax and freight on top of the ordered amount. Supply and as-needed contracts have ceilings that are limits on orders. Construction built in phases is funded phase by phase, and the Budget and Legislative Analyst notes that the Airport uses change orders this way. Where the excess is large the likeliest explanation is that the table is out of date, not that money left without authority: the source may be wrong rather than the conduct. What would settle a row: the contract's amendment history in the City's financial system. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
